namespaces.title: nc.logger
namespaces.text:
A console logger that works with zero setup: levels, colors, a small
markup for styling, groups, timers and tables. In production, switch to
one JSON object per line with `LOG_FORMAT=json`, and write to rotating
files if you need to.

Markup: `<% red bold Error:%> disk is full`. Any style name works, plus
`#ff8800`, `bg#1e1e2e`, `rgb(255, 128, 0)` and `bgRgb(...)`. Only the
first argument, the message, is read as markup: the values after it are
printed as they are.

What a terminal could act on is shown as text (`\x1b`, `\r`), so a logged
value can't move the cursor, change the title or forge a log line. Colors
from `nc.color`, links from `color.link()`, new lines and tabs still work,
and the lines of a message after its first one are indented, except with
`log()` when there is no scope and no timestamp.

Levels, from chatty to severe: `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`,
`fatal`. The default is `info`; `LOG_LEVEL` changes it. `DEBUG=1` shows
debug messages, and `DEBUG=db,http:*` only the debug and trace messages of
the loggers with these scopes. Warnings and errors go to stderr.

namespaces.title: nc.fs
namespaces.text:
Files and folders without try/catch: read and write text or JSON
(atomically), copy, move, delete, list, glob, watch, hash.

Paths: absolute paths are used as they are. Paths starting with `./` or
`../` start from the file that calls the function, so a script works
wherever it's run from. Other relative paths start from the working
directory, like Node's `fs`.

Everyday failures don't throw: you get `undefined` when something doesn't
exist and `false` when an operation fails.

namespaces.title: nc.checker
namespaces.text:
Type checks and validators. Every `isX` accepts anything and never throws,
and most of them are type guards: inside `if (nc.isString(value))`, your
editor knows `value` is a string, in JavaScript too.
examples:
if (nc.isEmail(body.email) && nc.isPort(body.port)) connect(body);
nc.assert(user, "User not found");

namespaces.title: nc.env
namespaces.text:
Environment variables you can trust: `.env` loading, typed getters, and
`validate()` to check your whole configuration at startup and report
every problem at once.

The `.env` file in the working directory is loaded when the package is
required; variables that are already set are never overwritten. Set
`NODE_COMFORT_DOTENV=false` to turn that off. What it loaded has the
lowest priority: a file you load yourself afterwards wins over it.

namespaces.title: nc.errors
namespaces.text:
The errors node-comfort throws when something goes wrong at run time: a
request fails, data is invalid, a command exits badly. They all extend
`NodeComfortError` (itself a regular `Error`) and carry a stable `code`,
so you can branch on the kind of failure without parsing messages.

A mistake in your own code, like a wrong argument, still throws a plain
`TypeError` or `RangeError`, as it does everywhere in JavaScript.

namespaces.title: nc.utils
namespaces.text:
Everyday helpers: `wait`, `when`, `dontCrash`, and JSON functions that
don't throw. They are also available at the top level (`nc.wait()`).

namespaces.title: nc.str
namespaces.text:
String helpers: case conversion, slugs, truncation, templates, wrapping,
fuzzy matching, plurals. Nothing is mutated, any value is accepted, and
lengths are counted the way you see them, so 👨‍👩‍👧 is one character and
is never cut in half.
examples:
str.slugify("Héllo, Wörld!");                    // "hello-world"
str.camelCase("user_first-name");                // "userFirstName"
str.plural(3, { one: "file", other: "files" }); // "3 files"

namespaces.title: nc.num
namespaces.text:
Numbers: clamping, rounding that gets decimals right, statistics, and
formatting for humans (sizes, money, ordinals, compact numbers) in any
language. Formatting is English by default: change it with `setLocale()`
or per call with `{ locale }`.
examples:
num.round(1.005, 2);                           // 1.01
num.formatBytes(1536);                         // "1.5 KB"
num.currency(1234.5, "EUR", { locale: "fr" }); // "1 234,50 €"
num.percentile(latencies, 95);

namespaces.title: nc.arr
namespaces.text:
Array helpers. None of them mutate what you pass in, and item types carry
through (`chunk(numbers, 2)` is a `number[][]`). Many take an iteratee:
a property name, which your editor completes, or a function.

namespaces.title: nc.obj
namespaces.text:
Object helpers: deep clone, merge, equality, diff, typed dot paths,
pick and omit. Inputs are never mutated, and `__proto__`, `constructor`
and `prototype` keys are always ignored, so user input can't pollute
prototypes.

namespaces.title: nc.time
namespaces.text:
Dates and durations: formatting, relative time, calendar math, time zones
and scheduling, in any language `Intl` knows. The default language is
English so results are the same on every machine; change it with
`setLocale()` or per call with `{ locale }`. Time zones work the same way
with `setTimezone()` or `{ timeZone }`.
examples:
time.setLocale("fr").setTimezone("Europe/Paris");
time.relative(Date.now() - 3600e3);        // "il y a 1 heure"
time.format(new Date(), "dddd D MMMM YYYY"); // "lundi 15 janvier 2024"
time.cron("0 9 * * 1-5", sendReport);        // weekdays at 9:00

namespaces.title: nc.id
namespaces.text:
Unique ids: UUID v4, v5 and v7, ULID, ObjectId, nanoid-style ids,
Snowflakes, tokens and short codes. Random ones use the secure generator
of `node:crypto`, with no bias.
examples:
id.uuidv7();         // "0190a5c4-7c1e-7b2a-9f3e-1c2d3e4f5a6b", sorts by creation time
id.nano();           // "V1StGXR8_Z5jdHi6B-myT"
id.prefixed("user"); // "user_7Hq2mXc0LrT9aZ4bWk1PdE8s"
id.code();           // "K7QF9X"
id.token(32);        // for API keys and reset links

namespaces.title: nc.schema
namespaces.text:
Validate data with schemas, in the spirit of `zod`. Describe your data
once and get both a runtime check with clear messages and the TypeScript
type, `Infer<typeof schema>`. Schemas never change: `.min()` or
`.optional()` return a new one.

namespaces.title: nc.func
namespaces.text:
Function helpers: debounce, throttle, memoize, retry with backoff,
timeouts, error handling without try/catch, and typed composition.

namespaces.title: nc.async
namespaces.text:
Promises and concurrency: map with a limit, queues with priorities,
mutexes, polling, and friendlier `Promise.allSettled`.

namespaces.title: nc.Cache
namespaces.text:
An in-memory cache with a size limit (the least recently used entries go
first), expiry per entry, and stats. `getOrSet()` loads a missing value
only once, even when many callers ask for it at the same moment.

namespaces.title: nc.Emitter
namespaces.text:
A small typed event emitter. Declare your events once, and your editor
checks every event name and listener argument. `on()` returns a function
that removes the listener, and you can `await` an event or loop over
events with `for await`.

namespaces.title: nc.http
namespaces.text:
An HTTP client on top of `fetch`: JSON by default, query objects, base
URLs, timeouts, safe retries that respect `Retry-After`, typed errors,
hooks, reusable clients and downloads with progress.

namespaces.title: nc.SQLite
namespaces.text:
SQLite made pleasant, on the engine built into Node.js: CRUD with
rich filters, JSON and boolean columns, transactions, migrations and
backups. Methods are synchronous, like the engine, but `await` still
works. Errors are `SQLiteError`s. Values are always bound as parameters
and names are checked, so there's no SQL injection through them.

namespaces.title: nc.cli
namespaces.text:
What you need for command-line tools: typed arguments with a generated
`--help`, prompts, arrow-key menus, spinners, progress bars, tables and
boxes. When nobody's at the keyboard (CI, pipes), prompts read plain lines
and animations print only their final state.

Tables, boxes, trees and menus show what a terminal could act on as text
(`\x1b`, `\r`), so a value can't move the cursor or break the layout.
Colors and links in them still work.

namespaces.title: nc.color
namespaces.text:
Terminal colors you can chain, like `chalk`. Truecolor is supported and
downgraded on older terminals. Colors switch off by themselves when the
output isn't a terminal or `NO_COLOR` is set; `FORCE_COLOR=1|2|3` turns
them back on.

namespaces.title: nc.sys
namespaces.text:
Processes and the system: run commands and get their output, find
executables, shut down cleanly, open URLs, and learn about the machine.
Behaves the same on Windows, macOS and Linux; on Windows,
`run("npm", [...])` finds `npm.cmd` and escapes arguments safely.

namespaces.title: nc.crypto
namespaces.text:
Crypto without the footguns, built on `node:crypto`: hashes, HMAC,
password hashing (scrypt or Argon2id), encryption (AES-256-GCM), JWT,
two-factor codes (TOTP) and secure random values.

symbols.name: isEmail
symbols.title: nc.checker.isEmail
symbols.text:
Does it look like an email address? The rules are practical rather than
the full RFC: one `@`, no stray dots, a real top-level domain.
International addresses are accepted, but not look-alike characters such
as the Kelvin sign in the domain. A valid address can still contain
quotes, `&`, `|` or backticks: it is not safe to put unescaped into HTML
or a shell command.
examples:
nc.isEmail("jose@exemple.fr");     // true
nc.isEmail("john..doe@example.com"); // false
nc.isEmail("john@localhost");       // false

symbols.name: isURL
symbols.title: nc.checker.isURL
symbols.text:
Is it an absolute URL with an allowed protocol (http and https by default)?
The text must already be clean: spaces, control characters, double

parser would quietly fix them. An apostrophe is fine.
examples:
nc.isURL("https://example.com/a?b=1");                 // true
nc.isURL("ftp://example.com", { protocols: ["ftp:"] }); // true
nc.isURL("http://localhost:3000", { requireTld: true }); // false

symbols.text:
Loads `.env` files into `process.env`. The first file to set a variable
wins, and variables that are already set are kept, unless you pass
`override`. The `.env` loaded by itself at startup doesn't count as
already set: `.env.local` wins over it, as you'd expect.

The load at startup leaves out the variables that can run code or weaken
TLS, and says so on stderr: `NODE_OPTIONS`, `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED`,
`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, `NODE_PATH`, `NODE_REDIRECT_WARNINGS`,
`NODE_REPL_EXTERNAL_MODULE`, `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`, `LD_PRELOAD`,
`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `LD_AUDIT`,
`DYLD_*`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_SSH`, `GIT_ASKPASS`, `GIT_EXEC_PATH`,
`GIT_CONFIG*`, `GIT_PROXY_COMMAND`, `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`, `GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR`,
`GIT_PAGER`, `GIT_EDITOR`, `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR`, `PAGER`, `EDITOR`,
`VISUAL`, `SSH_ASKPASS`, `PATH`, `PATHEXT`,
`ComSpec`, `BASH_ENV`, `PROMPT_COMMAND`, `PERL5OPT`,
`PYTHONSTARTUP`, `PYTHONPATH`, `RUBYOPT`, `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` and
`_JAVA_OPTIONS`. A call to `load()` loads them all: don't make one on a
file you don't trust, such as the `.env` of a repository someone sent you.
examples:
env.load();                                // ./.env
env.load([".env.local", ".env"]);          // local values win
env.load(".env.test", { override: true });
env.load(".env", { cascade: true });       // .env.production.local, .env.local, .env.production, .env

| Token | Output | | Token | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `YYYY` / `YY` | 2024 / 24 | | `HH` / `H` | 09 / 9 (24h) |
| `Q` | quarter, 1-4 | | `hh` / `h` | 09 / 9 (12h) |
| `MMMM` / `MMM` | January / Jan | | `mm` / `m` | 05 / 5 |
| `MM` / `M` | 01 / 1 | | `ss` / `s` | 07 / 7 |
| `DD` / `D` | 05 / 5 | | `SSS` | 042 (ms) |
| `dddd` / `ddd` | Monday / Mon | | `A` / `a` | PM / pm |
| `d` | weekday, 0 is Sunday | | `Z` / `ZZ` | +02:00 / +0200 |
| `W` / `WW` | ISO week | | `X` / `x` | Unix seconds / ms |
| `Do` | 5th | | `z` | zone name, like EST or GMT+1 |

Text in brackets stays as is: `"[Today is] dddd"`.
examples:
time.format(new Date(), "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss");                  // "2024-01-15 14:30:05"
time.format(Date.now(), "dddd D MMMM YYYY", { locale: "fr" });    // "lundi 15 janvier 2024"
time.format(Date.now(), "HH:mm Z", { timeZone: "Asia/Tokyo" });   // "22:30 +09:00"

symbols.name: nextRun
symbols.title: nc.time.nextRun

throws.text: If the expression is invalid.

symbols.text:
The next date matching a cron expression, without scheduling anything.

Expressions have 5 fields (`minute hour day month weekday`), or 6 with
seconds first. You can use `*`, lists (`1,15`), ranges (`1-5`), steps
(`*/15`), names (`jan`, `mon-fri`), `L` for the last day of the month,
and `@daily`, `@hourly`, `@weekly`, `@monthly`, `@yearly`. As in classic
cron, when both the day and the weekday are set, either one matching is
enough.
examples:
time.nextRun("0 9 * * mon-fri");                              // next weekday at 09:00
time.nextRun("0 0 1 * *", { timeZone: "America/New_York" });  // next 1st of the month

Compares two secrets in constant time, so the comparison can't leak

throws.text: If the settings are out of bounds, like a cost that needs more than 1 GiB of memory.

symbols.text:
Hashes a password with a random salt: scrypt by default, or Argon2id. The
result records its own settings, so you can raise the cost, or move to
Argon2id, later without breaking old hashes.

Argon2id hashes are standard PHC strings, readable by the other Argon2
libraries. Hashing and verifying them needs Node.js 24.7 or later; scrypt
works on every supported version.

symbols.name: verifyPassword

throws.text: If the hash asks for more work than allowed: scrypt with `p` over 16 or `128 * N * r * p` over 2**30 bytes (up to what version 2.1 accepted: past that, the hash is broken and gives `false`), Argon2 with more than 1 GiB of memory, 10 passes or 16 lanes. Rehash such passwords with settings within these limits.
With code `ERR_ARGON2_UNAVAILABLE` if the hash is Argon2 and this Node.js is older than 24.7. That is a deployment problem, not a wrong password, so it isn't hidden behind `false`.

symbols.text:
Checks a password against a stored hash, in constant time: scrypt hashes
from `hashPassword()`, and Argon2 PHC strings (`$argon2id$`, `$argon2i$`,

broken hash gives `false`. A hash asking for more work than allowed (more
than 1 GiB of memory, for instance) throws instead, without doing that
work: a doctored hash would stall the server that way, and a genuine one
isn't a wrong password but a hash to replace.
